summary: A University of Washington News article (Nov. 24, 2020) reports a study documenting 65 plant species that went extinct in the continental United States and Canada since European settlement, more than any previous scientific study. The study, led by Wesley Knapp of the North Carolina Natural Heritage Program with 16 experts including UW biology professor Richard Olmstead, was published Aug. 28 in Conservation Biology. The article notes two Washington extinctions, likely driven by land-use change, and argues that herbarium records and small-scale site protection are key to preventing future plant extinctions.
one_line: A 2020 study documents 65 plant species extinct in the continental US and Canada since European settlement, more than any prior study.
key_facts: A new study documents 65 plant species that have gone extinct in the continental United States and Canada since European settlement.
The study is described as having more extinctions than any previous scientific study has ever documented.
The study was led by Wesley Knapp of the North Carolina Natural Heritage Program and included a group of 16 experts from across the United States.
Richard Olmstead is a University of Washington professor of biology and curator of the UW's Burke Museum Herbarium and was a collaborator on the study.
The findings were published Aug. 28 in Conservation Biology.
The team found that most plant extinctions occurred in the western United States, where vegetation was minimally documented before widespread European settlement.
The article states the 65 documented extinctions likely underestimate the actual number of lost plant species.
In Washington state, the team found two confirmed extinctions: Astragalus kentrophyta var. douglasii (thistle milk-vetch) and Corispermum pallidum (pale bugseed).
Of the 65 documented extinctions, 64% were known only from a single location.
Corispermum pallidum was first collected in 1893 and was first described as a new species posthumously in 1995; the last known collection was from 1931.
Knapp said, "Preventing extinction is the lowest bar for conservation success we can set, yet we are not always successful."
Olmstead said, "There is no living memory of either of these species today."
Anne Frances, lead botanist at NatureServe, said, "In most cases, we can stop plants from going extinct, we just need the resources and commitment to do so."
The article attributes the Washington extinctions likely to the human impact of changing land use.
